entries.clue: One's time touring North Dakota with Jack, fine American, though old-fashioned (3-5)

annotation.definitionNote: Only 'fine' is the sense; 'American' and 'though old-fashioned' are usage labels, marking the word as a US colloquialism that has had a dated ring for decades.

indicatorNotes.touring: A tourist goes round a place rather than into it, so the word it governs travels all the way around the letters named next.

blocks.note: j = jack, the card between ten and queen
'one is' contracts to I'm
a day is a measure of time, and it opens up to take the state in
ND is the two-letter postal code for North Dakota

annotation.surface: Someone spends a day driving round North Dakota in Jack's company.
annotation.walkthrough: 'One's' looks like a possessive and has to be heard as 'one is'. The jack leads the answer even though the clue mentions him last, after the day out.
annotation.definitionFit: Jim-dandy is American slang for something first-rate, a fine specimen of its kind, and it has sounded quaint since about the 1950s.

entries.clue: Juliet Seaman makes punch (3)

blocks.note: Juliet is J in the radio alphabet
an AB is an able seaman, the Navy's rating for a trained sailor

annotation.surface: A woman called Juliet Seaman lands one on somebody.
annotation.walkthrough: The capital letters on 'Seaman' are the disguise: it is a rank, not a surname. A jab is thrown with the leading hand and is the shortest punch in boxing.
annotation.definitionFit: A jab is a short straight punch delivered with the front hand, so the plain noun swaps in.

entries.clue: Dull-looking, uniform dress in the Middle Ages (7)

indicatorNotes.in the Middle: What is in the middle of a word is its centre and neither of its ends, so only the inside letters are wanted.

blocks.note: a mat finish is flat and unshiny, the dull-looking one
Uniform is U in the radio alphabet
the three letters at the centre of dRESs

annotation.surface: Drab, identical clothing of the sort worn in medieval times.
annotation.walkthrough: 'The Middle Ages' is one phrase on the surface doing two separate jobs underneath: 'in the Middle' hollows out DRESS, and 'Ages' is the definition left standing on its own.
annotation.definitionFit: Cheese, wine and people all mature as they age, so the verb swaps straight in for 'ages' in the same tense.

entries.clue: Before noon, work steadily enough (5)

blocks.note: am is ante meridiem, the hours before midday
to ply a trade is to keep working away at it

annotation.surface: Putting in a solid stretch of work before lunchtime.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Enough' reads as the tail of the sentence about the morning's work and is the definition standing alone. Ply survives mostly in 'plying a trade' and in the plier of oars.
annotation.definitionFit: Amply means to a sufficient degree, so 'paid amply' and 'paid enough' make the same claim.

entries.clue: God knows, ultimately, who rigged event where setters may win awards (3,4)

annotation.definition: event where setters may win awards

indicatorNotes.rigged: A rigged contest has been tampered with so the result comes out other than it should, which is what happens to these letters.
indicatorNotes.ultimately: Ultimately means at the very end, and the very end of a word is its final letter.

blocks.note: the three letters of GOD in a new order
the final letter of knows
the three letters of WHO in a new order

annotation.surface: A shrug of exasperation about who fixed some competition.
annotation.walkthrough: Setters are the gun dogs here — Irish, English, Gordon — not the people who write crosswords. One 'rigged' does duty twice over, on God and on who.
annotation.definitionFit: A dog show is a judged event at which breeds including setters take the rosettes, so the definition describes the answer rather than translating it.

entries.clue: Spoil drop of Courvoisier brandy (4)

indicatorNotes.drop of: A drop of something is the smallest part of it, which for a word is the single letter it starts with.

blocks.note: to mar something is to spoil it
the opening letter of Courvoisier

annotation.surface: Ruining a small measure of expensive cognac.
annotation.walkthrough: Marc is distilled from the skins and pips left in the press after the wine is made — the rough end of the trade, where Courvoisier sits at the smooth end.
annotation.definitionFit: Marc is a brandy, the spirit French growers distil from pressed grape residue, so the category word defines it.

entries.clue: Kind of crack (not heroin) that gets people high? (7)

annotation.definitionNote: The definition is a relative clause standing in for a noun — the thing that does this — and it works by what the answer does rather than by any synonym.

indicatorNotes.not: Not marks the piece that follows as one to be left out rather than added in.

blocks.note: a hairline crack is the finest kind, the one you can barely see
h = heroin in street usage, and it is the letter that goes

annotation.surface: A dealer clarifying which sort of crack is on offer.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Crack' pulls towards drugs and heroin holds you there; the crack wanted is the one in a windscreen. The question mark covers 'high' meaning altitude.
annotation.definitionFit: An airline's business is carrying passengers several miles up, so 'high' is meant literally rather than chemically.

entries.clue: Reportedly grab a dal, when served up - it's healthy-ish food (6,5)

indicatorNotes.Reportedly: Reportedly means as the thing is said rather than as it is written, so you spell out what the ear receives.
indicatorNotes.served up: In a down clue something served up has been turned over, so its letters are read from the bottom back to the top.

blocks.note: to grab is to seize, and 'seize a' said aloud is the emperor's name
dal is the Indian dish of split lentils
as does the work of when in 'as I arrived'

annotation.surface: Someone mishears an instruction to grab a portion of lentils as it arrives.
annotation.walkthrough: Two halves, two devices: the first is a sound, the second a pair of words turned upside down. 'When' pulling its weight as AS is the piece solvers miss.
annotation.definitionFit: A Caesar salad is nominally salad, but the parmesan, croutons and creamy dressing keep it well short of virtuous — hence the hedge.

entries.clue: An objection to border (4)

blocks.note: an shortens to the single article a
'but' is the word people raise an objection with

annotation.surface: One complaint lodged against a frontier.
annotation.walkthrough: The objection is not described but quoted: 'but' is the word itself, the one that arrives whenever somebody is about to disagree.
annotation.definitionFit: To abut something is to border it, sharing an edge with it, so the two verbs swap in unchanged.

entries.clue: Gripping work, being assistant to pianist (4-6)

blocks.note: the book you cannot put down
the person sitting beside the stool at a recital

annotation.surface: An absorbing job helping out a concert pianist.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Work' is the hinge: it points at a book, not at employment, and the clue then quietly supplies the employment in its second half.
annotation.definitionFit: A page-turner is a book too gripping to put down, and it is also the recital assistant who turns the sheet music for the player.

entries.clue: Fly over to catch a one-time Queen singer in America (7)

indicatorNotes.over: Something turned over lies the other way up, so in a down clue these letters are read from the bottom.
indicatorNotes.to catch: To catch a thing is to have it in your grasp, so the letters just named close around what comes next.

blocks.note: the fly is a gnat, written backwards
the word is taken at face value as the letter
ER is Elizabeth Regina, and 'one-time' marks a reign that has ended

annotation.surface: Flying out to catch a former Queen vocalist playing in the States.
annotation.walkthrough: Queen is the band on the surface and the monarch underneath, shortened to ER. 'One-time' is there because Elizabeth II's reign is over, not because the singer left the group.
annotation.definitionFit: Tanagers are the bright-plumaged American songbirds — scarlet, summer, western — so 'singer' gives the family and 'in America' says where to look.

entries.clue: Bright red tracks alongside Red River (6)

blocks.note: Che Guevara, the revolutionary a crossword calls a Red
r = river, as on a map
ry is the short form of railway, whose tracks these are

annotation.surface: Crimson rails running beside a river called the Red.
annotation.walkthrough: A crossword Red is usually a communist, and Che Guevara is the three-letter one. The tracks are named first in the clue but sit last in the answer.
annotation.definitionFit: Cherry is the vivid red of the ripe fruit, the shade meant by a cherry-red car or lipstick.

entries.clue: Our horse goes wild with Bovril - oddly, horses being this? (11)

annotation.definitionNote: The setter defines by pointing rather than by synonym: the last three words say the answer is the thing horses are, and the question mark admits the sleight.

indicatorNotes.goes wild: Something that goes wild stops keeping to the order it was put in, and letters that go wild land somewhere new.
indicatorNotes.oddly: Oddly points at the odd positions — first, third, fifth — and takes only the letters standing there.

blocks.note: anagram fodder, 8 letters
the first, third and fifth letters of BOVRIL

annotation.surface: The family horse gets excited at the sight of a jar of Bovril.
annotation.walkthrough: Bovril is the British beef extract stirred into hot water, which is exactly what no horse would touch — the surface contradicts the answer on purpose.
annotation.definitionFit: A herbivorous animal lives on plants alone, which is what horses do: grass, hay, oats and nothing made of beef.

entries.clue: In speech, convenient to limit hindrance (8)

indicatorNotes.In speech: In speech means as the word is said rather than as it is written, so the sound is what gets spelt out.

blocks.note: convenient is handy, and its sound is written with an i here
a cap is the limit set on a fee or a bonus

annotation.surface: Talk of something convenient that keeps a nuisance within bounds.
annotation.walkthrough: Only the first half is sounded out; the cap arrives spelt as it comes. A cap is the ceiling put on a price or a headcount, nothing to do with hats.
annotation.definitionFit: A handicap is whatever holds you back, so 'hindrance' is the plain noun for the same thing.

entries.clue: Weapon that's Spooner's chief boast (8)

indicatorNotes.Spooner's: Spooner's version of a phrase swaps the opening sounds of its two words, so trade the beginnings of the pair that follows.

blocks.note: the chief is the boss and to boast is to crow, and their opening sounds change places

annotation.surface: The head man's bragging, as the Reverend Spooner might have reported it.
annotation.walkthrough: The Reverend William Spooner was an Oxford warden whose tangled tongue gave the device its name. Crowing is the boasting sense, as in crowing over a win.
annotation.definitionFit: A crossbow is a weapon: a short bow fixed across a stock and fired from the shoulder like a rifle.

entries.clue: Commotion dogs British party lacking energy and swagger (7)

indicatorNotes.dogs: Something that dogs you comes along at your heels, so this piece trails the letters named after it.
indicatorNotes.lacking: Lacking says a named piece is missing from the word beside it, not added to it.

blocks.note: b = British
a rave is an all-night dance party
e = energy, the letter the party loses
ado is a fuss or commotion, as in much ado about nothing

annotation.surface: Trouble follows a British political party that has run out of steam.
annotation.walkthrough: The party the surface offers is a political one and the party wanted is a rave. 'Dogs' is the verb — trouble dogging someone — and it settles which piece trails which.
annotation.definitionFit: Bravado is boldness put on for show with nothing behind it, and a swagger is the same bluster carried in the walk.

entries.clue: Rock singles left out to be sorted (6)

indicatorNotes.left out: Left out says a piece is omitted, and the piece omitted is the L that 'left' itself stands for.
indicatorNotes.to be sorted: Sorting a pile is putting it into an order it was not in before, which is what happens to these letters.

blocks.note: the word handed over whole, before the deletion
l = left, the letter dropped from SINGLES

annotation.surface: Rock records nobody bought, lying about waiting to be filed.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Left' has to be read as the letter L before 'out' can throw it away. Gneiss is the coarse banded rock of the Scottish Highlands, and it is said 'nice'.
annotation.definitionFit: Gneiss is a rock: the banded metamorphic kind formed deep down under heat and pressure, so the definition gives only the category.

entries.clue: Area covered by dish which is round or square (6)

indicatorNotes.covered by: Whatever is covered by something has that thing spread over and around it, so the letter goes inside.

blocks.note: a pizza is the round dish, and the insertion splits it after two letters
a = area

annotation.surface: A pizza wide enough to blanket the whole area.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Round' belongs to the dish rather than to the shape of the answer, which is the trap. Pizza and piazza differ by one letter, and the clue puts that letter in.
annotation.definitionFit: A piazza is the open public square of an Italian town, the one the cafes and the cathedral face onto.

entries.clue: Crash when small weight's upended on head, sustaining stunning blow (4,3)

indicatorNotes.upended: Something upended has been stood on its head, so in a down clue its letters run the other way.
indicatorNotes.on: In a down entry a piece sitting on another rests above it, so this one goes in first.
indicatorNotes.sustaining: To sustain a blow is to take it and carry it, so the blow ends up inside the word that takes it.

blocks.note: oz is the ounce, the small weight, stood on its head
nut is slang for the head, as in nutting someone
a KO is a knockout, the blow that stuns

annotation.surface: A weight tips over onto someone's head and lays them out.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Crash' is the sofa sense — falling asleep where you land — not a collision, and 'sustaining' plays both ways at once, taking a blow and holding one inside.
annotation.definitionFit: To zonk out is to drop into heavy sleep on the spot, which is what 'crash' means in crashing on someone's couch.

entries.clue: Climb that is followed by walk (8)

blocks.note: sc. is the Latin scilicet, the footnote's 'that is to say'
a ramble is a walk taken for pleasure in the country

annotation.surface: A steep ascent with a gentler stroll to follow.
annotation.walkthrough: 'That is' looks like the clue's grammar rather than a piece of the answer, which is where the difficulty sits. Scilicet is rarer in print than i.e. but means the same.
annotation.definitionFit: A scramble is a climb up ground rough and steep enough to need hands as well as feet.

entries.clue: The foremost of St Andrew's legacies - flag displaying cross (7)

indicatorNotes.The foremost of: The foremost of anything is what stands at its front, and the front of each word named is its first letter.

blocks.note: the opening letters of St, Andrew's and legacies
to flag is to tire, to lose your energy on a long day

annotation.surface: The chief bequest of St Andrew is a flag with a cross on it.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Flag' is the verb, meaning to tire, while the surface keeps it as the thing on the pole. St Andrew was said to be martyred on a diagonal cross, which is why Scotland's flag carries one.
annotation.definitionFit: A saltire is a cross with its arms set diagonally, the heraldic X that Scotland flies in white on blue.

entries.clue: Heron flapping after second bird (7)

indicatorNotes.flapping: Something flapping is beating about loose, so its letters will not stay in the order they were given.
indicatorNotes.after: After puts the letters just described behind the piece named next, not in front of it.

blocks.note: a mo is a moment, the informal second of 'hang on a mo'
anagram fodder, 5 letters

annotation.surface: A heron takes off a second behind another bird.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Second' is the MO of 'half a mo', not the ordinal. Two waterbirds in one clue, and the big one supplies the letters for the small one.
annotation.definitionFit: 'Bird' is the bare category: the answer is the dark waterbird with the red-and-yellow bill seen on English ponds and canals.

entries.clue: County Kerry's neighbour cut large grassy area back (8)

indicatorNotes.cut: Something cut has had its end taken off, so the last letter of the word named goes.
indicatorNotes.back: Back turns the letters just assembled round to read the other way.

blocks.note: Cork is the Irish county next door to Kerry, cut short by a letter
l = large, as on a clothing label
a lawn is the mown grassy area of a garden

annotation.surface: Trimming a big stretch of grass next door to County Kerry.
annotation.walkthrough: Kerry and Cork are Irish counties and the answer is an English one, which is the jump the clue hides. 'Cut' reads as mowing and means docking a letter.
annotation.definitionFit: Cornwall is the county at the south-western tip of England, so 'County' names the category the answer belongs to.

entries.clue: Carpets flogged at opening of store, about a hundred (6)

indicatorNotes.opening of: The opening of a word is the letter it begins with and nothing more.
indicatorNotes.about: To be about something is to be wrapped round it, so the letters already assembled close over the one that follows.

blocks.note: flogged is sold, in the market-stall sense
the first letter of store
C is a hundred in Roman numerals

annotation.surface: Rugs going cheap in a shop's launch sale at around a hundred pounds.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Carpets' is the British verb: to carpet someone is to call them in and tell them off, a dressing-down on the boss's rug. 'Flogged' is selling, not beating.
annotation.definitionFit: To carpet somebody is British idiom for hauling them in for a telling-off, which is scolding them, and both verbs are third-person singular.

entries.clue: Radioed co-ordinates in time for drops (5)

indicatorNotes.Radioed: Something radioed arrives as sound over the air, so what you spell is what the ear takes in.

blocks.note: to sync things is to co-ordinate them in time, and the word is heard rather than read

annotation.surface: A ship's position is transmitted at the agreed moment.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Co-ordinates' reads as map references and is the verb, short for synchronises. 'Radioed' is quietly doing the job 'sounds like' usually does.
annotation.definitionFit: Something that sinks drops — the sun sinks behind the hill, prices sink — so the two verbs match in sense and in tense.

entries.clue: Moonlit, cool, unending swirls having power to move (10)

indicatorNotes.unending: What is unending has no end, so the final letter of the word named is taken off.
indicatorNotes.swirls: A swirl spins things round until they settle somewhere new, which is what becomes of these letters.

blocks.note: anagram fodder, 7 letters
COOL without its last letter

annotation.surface: A cool moonlit night over endlessly swirling water.
annotation.walkthrough: The comma after 'cool' is what tells you 'unending' docks that word and not the swirls. Loco- is Latin for place, the same root that gives the locomotive its name.
annotation.definitionFit: Locomotion is the power of moving from one place to another, the capacity rather than any particular movement.

entries.clue: Beautiful goddess imprisoned by the Beast (4)

indicatorNotes.imprisoned by: What is imprisoned is shut inside its surroundings, so the letters sit unbroken within the words that follow.

blocks.note: tHE BEast, running across the gap between the words

annotation.surface: Beauty is locked up by the Beast, as the fairy tale has it.
annotation.walkthrough: Beauty and the Beast is the story the surface tells, and the goddess wanted is hiding inside the monster's half of the title.
annotation.definitionFit: Hebe is the Greek goddess of youth, cupbearer to the Olympians, and her name is the word for the bloom of early life.

entries.clue: Rotten fish brought up (3)

indicatorNotes.brought up: In a down clue something brought up is carried back towards the top, so its letters read upwards.

blocks.note: a dab is a small flatfish, read upwards

annotation.surface: A spoiled fish hauled back up onto the deck.
annotation.walkthrough: A dab is a small North Sea flatfish, common on British fishmongers' slabs and commoner still in crosswords, where three letters count for a lot.
annotation.definitionFit: Bad is the word for food that has gone off — a bad egg, bad milk — which is rotten in the everyday kitchen sense.

entries.clue: When caught, go down burrow (4)

indicatorNotes.When caught: To catch what somebody says is to hear it, so what is wanted is the sound of the word and not its usual spelling.

blocks.note: the sun goes down when it sets, and the sound takes a second t here

annotation.surface: A hunted animal dives underground the moment it is spotted.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Caught' is the homophone signal, in the sense of catching what was said. Badgers are the only British animal whose home takes the doubled spelling.
annotation.definitionFit: A sett is a badger's burrow, the tunnelled chamber system it digs out and lives in for generations.

entries.clue: Rise as one, determined, but not fully experienced (8)

indicatorNotes.not fully: Not fully says the words carrying the answer are used only in part, so a run of letters is taken out of the middle of them.

blocks.note: riSE AS ONE Determined, straight across the words and the comma

annotation.surface: A crowd gets to its feet together, resolute but holding something back.
annotation.walkthrough: Nothing here looks like an anagram or a container, and 'not fully' is the only instruction — easy to read as more of the sentence about being determined.
annotation.definitionFit: A seasoned campaigner is an experienced one: time and use season soldiers and timber alike.
